title: Stochastic arrival: batch & concurrency sensitivity matrix (draft)
body:
Purpose
-----
This is a working note describing a spreadsheet layout and an experiment matrix to evaluate the joint effect of stochastic arrivals, batching windows, and concurrency sizing on throughput, p95 latency, and per-token cost. The goal: create a compact sensitivity matrix that feeds the Optimize team’s recommendation engine and can be exported as a canonical CSV for customer sizing docs.

Context / motivation
--------------------
- We repeatedly get requests asking: what concurrency and batching window should a customer pick for X qps and Y median token length?
- Prior notes focus on deterministic sizing or single-scenario continuous-batching curves. This doc explores a small but representative search space using stochastic arrival traces and a Monte Carlo-backed spreadsheet that produces p50/p95/p99 and cost bands.

High-level approach (spreadsheet design)
--------------------------------------
Tabs (recommended):
1) params - inputs and global constants (GPU $/hr, slot counts, kernel profile names)
2) workload-scenarios - arrival rates, arrival distribution types (Poisson/Weibull/bursty), token length distributions, prefix-cache hit rate
3) service-model - per-GPU effective token throughput table by batch size and sequence length (empirical kernels)
4) queue-sim - Monte Carlo simulator outputs by scenario x (batch-window, concurrency, max-batch)
5) summary - sensitivity matrix with cells = {p95 latency, throughput, cost_per_1M_tokens, risk_flag}
6) recommendations - human-friendly configs and notes for each SLA tier

Key spreadsheet fields/formulas (pseudo-sheet)
-------------------------------------------
- Effective service rate (tokens/sec) per GPU given batch size B:
  SERVICE_RATE(B) = measured_tokens_per_sec(B) * kernel_efficiency_factor (from service-model tab)
- Arrival intensity (tokens/sec) = requests_per_sec * mean_tokens_per_request
- Expected batches/sec (approx) = min(concurrency * SERVICE_RATE(B) / mean_tokens_per_batch, arrival_tokens/sec / mean_tokens_per_batch)
- Approx p95 latency estimate (analytic fallback): use Erlang-C-like formula adapted for variable service times and batching:
  P95_lat = queue_wait_quantile(0.95, lambda, mu_effective, c) + average_batching_delay(B, T_window) + network_overhead_ms
  (sheet: if simulated sample count < threshold then fallback_to_analytic = TRUE)
- Cost / 1M tokens = (n_gpus * GPU_$per_hr * runtime_hours) / (tokens_processed / 1e6)

Notes on queueing model choices
-------------------------------
- Arrival process: real traffic is not perfectly Poisson. Include: Poisson, bursty (gamma/Weibull interarrival), and peak-within-minute spikes (Markov-modulated Poisson).
- Service time: measured in tokens per second, but distribution is heavy-tailed because of variable sequence length. Instead of assuming M/M/c, approximate M/G/c and use an empirical service-time distribution in Monte Carlo.
- We will compute Erlang-C baseline for quick cells; Monte Carlo overrides for final cells where variance matters. Include a column 'analytic_error_margin' showing (sim_p95 - erlangC_p95).

Batching window and effective batching delay
-----------------------------------------
- Two knobs: max_batch_size B and batching window T_ms.
- Average batching delay depends on arrival rate and T_ms; sheet uses Poisson interarrival approximation to compute expected wait for B or T_ms whichever comes first.
- Important: high T_ms increases p95 nonlinearly under low qps/high tokens workloads (because batches fill slowly).

Example sensitivity slice (toy numbers, replace with measured kernels)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Columns: scenario, qps, mean_tokens, concurrency c, max_batch B, T_window(ms), p50_ms, p95_ms, throughput_tokens_sec, cost_per_1M_tokens
Rows (examples):
- S1: qps=12 req/s, mean_tokens=120, c=8, B=48, T=30ms -> p95=210ms, throughput=63k tokens/s, cost_per_1M=$0.58
- S2: qps=12 req/s, mean_tokens=120, c=4, B=96, T=80ms -> p95=390ms (queue dominated), throughput=70k tokens/s, cost_per_1M=$0.45 (but p95>300ms)
- S3: qps=60 req/s, mean_tokens=40, c=16, B=32, T=10ms -> p95=140ms, throughput=95k tokens/s, cost_per_1M=$0.48

Interpretation: smaller batch windows and more concurrency reduce p95 at cost of GPU efficiency and therefore unit cost. Larger B improves throughput and cheapens cost but risks higher p95 during slow arrival periods.

Risk and caveats
----------------
- Kernel throughput numbers must be empirical per-model and per-hardware. The spreadsheet assumes we already have per-B empirical tokens/sec for the model-family. If not available, the cost numbers are meaningless.
- Erlang-C overestimates p95 when service time variance is low, underestimates when heavy tailed. Monte Carlo is necessary for customer-facing recommendations.
- KV/prefix cache effect: cached prefixes reduce service time dramatically for long conversations; include a 'cache_hit_rate' knob and apply multiplicative reduction on mean_tokens and variance.

Planned experiments to populate the sheet (lab tasks)
--------------------------------------------------
1) Kernel sweep: run perf harness for model-family X on rtx-a100-40GB with B in {8,16,32,48,64,96}. Produce tokens/sec, latency-dist per batch size. (owner: Marisol, due: 2025-11-27)
2) Arrival trace replay: replay three production traces (steady, diurnal, spike) through the simulator; collect simulated p50/p95/p99 for (c,B,T) grid. (owner: Ethan, due: 2025-12-05)
3) Live smoke test: pick 2 recommended configs from summary tab and run canary on dedicated pool with synthetic load to measure real p95 and batch distribution. (owner: Priya, due: 2025-12-12)
4) Build automation: script to render sheet -> CSV -> JSON that Optimize can ingest. (owner: Alexei, due: 2025-12-15)

Actionable outputs (what this spreadsheet must produce)
-----------------------------------------------------
- Sensitivity matrix CSV with keys: scenario_id, s3 (qps,mean_tokens,arrival_model), c, B, T, empirical_p95_ms, throughput_tokens_s, cost_per_1M, cache_hit_rate_assumption, risk_flag
- For each scenario choose 3 recommended configs: latency-first, cost-first, balanced. Include why each was chosen (short bullet).

Unresolved questions / TODOs
--------------------------
- How do we incorporate heterogeneous workloads (mix of short/long requests) into a single cell? Suggest weighted-mix scenarios but need product input on realistic mixes.
- Should we add a knob for preemption-priority (priority queues for interactive traffic)? That impacts effective concurrency; needs SRE input.
- How to express confidence bounds programmatically so Optimize can warn customers if p95 has >10% simulation variance?

Immediate next steps (this week)
--------------------------------
- Finalize spreadsheet tab layout and column names (Ethan)
- Kick off kernel sweep (Marisol)
- Add one real production trace to linked_artifacts and sanity-run sim.

Notes to reviewers
------------------
- This is a rough working draft intended to converge into an Optimize ingestible CSV schema. Please comment directly in the sheet linked in linked_artifacts and tag me. If you have a preferred analytic fallback to Erlang-C or approximations you've used before, paste formula snippets into the params tab.

Appendix: quick formulas and heuristics (copy into sheet)
--------------------------------------------------------
- mean_batch_fill_time_approx = (B / arrival_rate_reqs) * mean_tokens_per_req / mean_tokens_per_batch  (use only for rough bounds)
- empirical_cost_estimate = (GPU_$hr * 3600) / (SERVICE_RATE(B) * 3600) * 1e6 / tokens_processed -> simplifies to GPU_$hr * 1e6 / tokens_processed_per_hr
- fallback_p95_erlangC = erlangC_quantile(0.95, lambda_requests, mu_requests, c) + avg_batch_delay_ms + network_ms

Owner and reviewers
-------------------
- Owner: Ethan Chen (eng-serving-runtime)
- Reviewers: Priya Raman (optimize), Marisol Vega (perf), Alexei Petrov (sre)
